analysis.one_liner: Requires health plans to prove their mental health coverage limits match medical coverage limits.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 60 cosponsors from both parties but never left committee; its only action beyond referral was one subcommittee hearing, and it died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law already says insurance that covers mental health and substance use care cannot make it harder to get than physical care. But insurers can also block care with practices like prior authorization, which are harder to measure. This bill would have required health plans to write up and hand federal officials a comparison showing those practices are applied no more strictly to mental health care, and it would have made the government check plans' paperwork every year and report the results to Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: People whose health insurance covers mental health or substance use treatment — especially those denied care or made to wait because of prior authorization or similar plan rules. The bill would give the Department of Health and Human Services a way to see whether a plan's mental health rules are stricter than its medical rules, flag plans that get complaints, and publish findings to Congress and the states. Mental health and addiction treatment providers would also likely gain, since easier access to covered care means more patients able to use their benefits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People whose insurance covers mental health care

how_it_helps.text: Requires every group health plan and insurer that covers both medical and mental health benefits to prepare a detailed comparison showing that non-quantitative limits on mental health care — such as prior authorization rules — are designed and applied no more strictly than the equivalent limits on medical and surgical care.

Makes those comparisons available to the government on request, starting within 60 days of a request in 2020 and immediately beginning in 2021, so regulators can inspect them rather than take a plan's word.

Directs HHS to demand a plan's analysis whenever the department has received complaints about that plan's mental health or substance use benefits, and to request analyses from at least 50 randomly selected plans every year.

Requires an annual public report to Congress listing which plans submitted adequate analyses, which were out of compliance, and what they were told to fix, with noncompliance also shared with inspectors general and the states.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employers that sponsor group health plans would bear the cost of preparing and producing the comparative analyses and of changing plan rules if regulators found their mental health limits too strict. Those administrative costs would partly flow into premiums. People currently denied mental health care pay today in the form of untreated conditions and out-of-pocket costs; the bill was aimed at shifting some of that burden back onto the plans.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and employer health plans

drawbacks.text: The bill creates no new penalties: if HHS finds a plan out of compliance, it can only specify what the plan must do, and the text provides no fines or enforcement trigger beyond disclosure and reporting.

Enforcement depends heavily on the complaint system and on HHS actually reviewing analyses from the 50 random plans and every complained-about plan each year, so the bill's real-world effect would rise or fall with the department's resources and diligence.
Insurers and employers would face real administrative costs to document and justify every treatment limitation, and those compliance costs could be passed into premiums for all enrollees.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea is sound and modest: parity law is hard to enforce when the discriminatory limits are invisible, and forcing plans to document them is the standard first step. The main weakness is that the bill is all paperwork and reporting — no penalties for noncompliance — so a noncompliant insurer could face an unfavorable report but nothing binding. It would have been a genuine but limited improvement for people fighting mental health denials, at a real but ordinary compliance cost to the industry.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in three House committees for about 18 months, got a single subcommittee hearing, and expired when the Congress ended without ever reaching a committee or floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Katie Porter introduced the bill on June 10, 2019 with Reps. Gus Bilirakis, a Republican, and Donald Norcross as original cosponsors.

The Speaker referred it to three committees at once — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and Labor — a split that means no single committee owns the bill and each must act before it can advance.
The next day it was sent to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee, where it stayed.
The subcommittee held a hearing on June 30, 2020 — the last recorded action on the bill.
No committee ever voted to send it to the floor and the full House never voted on it; it died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employer health plans are better off because the bill died — they never had to produce comparative analyses of their mental health limits or answer to regulators for them. People with mental health and substance use coverage gained nothing from the outcome.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was bipartisan — 51 of 231 House Democrats and 9 of 197 House Republicans — but the bill skewed Democratic, and since no committee or floor vote ever happened, there is no record of how the parties would have split on passage.

industries.note: The bill would have forced insurers to document and justify the prior authorization and other limits they place on mental health care, and to submit to annual government review when complaints arise. Insurers benefit today from limits that are hard to challenge because they are never written down and compared, which is exactly what the bill targeted.

industries.industry: Employers that sponsor group health plans
industries.note: Self-insured employer plans would have had to prepare the same comparative analyses and respond to regulator requests. The burden is administrative, and many employers pass compliance costs into the benefits they offer workers.

industries.industry: Mental health and addiction treatment providers
industries.note: If plans could no longer quietly apply stricter limits to mental health care, more patients could actually use their covered benefits, expanding the pool of people able to access and pay for treatment.
